name: Weight cycling (bulk-cut)

lead: Bulk-cut cycling means spending a period eating above maintenance to add muscle (and some fat), then a period eating below maintenance to lose fat while keeping the muscle.

The payoff is a bigger, leaner physique: lifters add size in the surplus and show definition after the deficit. Bodybuilders typically bulk in an off-season and cut around 12 to 14 weeks before a show.

paras: Lifters track body weight and calories, run a surplus during bulks (clean or dirty), then a deficit during cuts, with resistance training throughout. Some use lean bulks or maintenance breaks to limit fat gain.

Larger surpluses add more fat. Observational data link weight fluctuation to poorer health outcomes, but a 2026 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology review judged evidence does not support causal harm from cycling itself. Extreme water cuts in combat sports raise separate concerns.

chain: A calorie surplus with resistance training adds muscle
A following deficit strips the fat gained alongside it
A larger, leaner, more defined body with each round
angle.text: Bulking supplies the energy to add muscle, and cutting removes fat so the muscle shows, which is why lifters alternate the two to build size and definition over a period of years [1][8]. Looksmaxxing users apply the same pattern to reach a target body-fat level and a fuller physique [2].

lead: Weight cycling in lifting culture, usually called bulking and cutting, is the deliberate alternation of a calorie-surplus phase (the bulk) with a calorie-deficit phase (the cut). The bulk is used to add muscle; the cut is used to lose the fat gained along the way and show the muscle underneath, so that repeated rounds build a bigger and more defined physique over time [1][2][3].

The structure comes from competitive bodybuilding, where athletes build mass for most of the year in an off-season and begin cutting roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest [1]. Recreational lifters and looksmaxxing forum members borrow the rhythm, asking at what body-fat percentage to stop bulking and start cutting, and how long each phase should run [4]. A 'clean bulk' uses a small, tracked surplus to limit fat gain; a 'dirty bulk' uses a large, loosely tracked one that adds weight quickly [1][5].

Outside lifting, repeated loss and regain of weight is known as weight cycling or yo-yo dieting, and has been studied mainly in people with obesity. A 2024 systematic review of 23 studies found that most did not show added fat, lost lean mass or lower resting metabolic rate after weight cycling [6], and a 2026 Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology review concluded that current evidence does not support a causal link between weight cycling itself and clinical harm [7]. Meta-analyses of observational data, by contrast, associate weight fluctuation with higher cardiovascular and all-cause mortality [8].
infobox: Clean (tracked, small surplus), dirty (large, loose surplus) [1]
About 10-20% above maintenance for novice/intermediate lifters; lower for advanced [2]
About 0.5-1% of body weight per week [9]
Yo-yo dieting, recomposition, mini-cut, reverse dieting

paras: Bulking is eating above maintenance calories with heavy resistance training; larger surpluses and longer bulks add more fat alongside muscle. Cutting is eating below maintenance; a bigger deficit loses weight faster but raises the risk of losing muscle [1].

Variants are discussed widely. A clean bulk keeps the surplus modest, tracks macronutrients and tends to take longer; a dirty bulk uses a large, minimally tracked surplus, often with energy-dense food, and usually calls for a harder cut afterwards [1]. Lifters also describe lean bulking, short 'mini-cuts' between bulks, maintenance breaks and 'reverse dieting', the gradual raising of calories after a cut. Competitors add a final contest stage of carbohydrate loading, dehydration, tanning and shaving [1].
Reviews on bodybuilding nutrition describe the phases: an off-season built around a modest surplus, a contest-preparation phase of a deficit with cardio, and a post-contest recovery phase [2][9][10].

Wikipedia dates the vocabulary of 'bulking up' and 'cutting down' to the 1950s and 1960s, popularised through bodybuilding magazines and physique contests [1]. A 2022 article in The Conversation by Lancaster University physiologist Christopher Gaffney likewise traces the method to 1960s bodybuilders and notes that it remains popular among amateurs [3].

As bodybuilding spread through gyms and later online forums, the pattern moved from contest athletes to general lifters. A looksmax.org thread titled 'When do you Bulk/Cut?' shows a typical question: whether a man at about 20% body fat should cut to roughly 10 to 12% first, then bulk to 16% and repeat, or tolerate more fat [4]. A reply in that thread suggests that someone new to lifting could lose fat first and then use a surplus to take advantage of 'noob gains' [4].

Practitioners track body weight (often as a weekly average), photographs and body-fat estimates, and decide when to change phase by those markers. Typical durations vary: Gaffney describes bulks of about 4 to 6 weeks and cuts of 6 to 8 weeks in amateur routines [3], whereas contest cuts traditionally run two to four months [9].

Narrative reviews by physique-sport researchers give general ranges for context. For off-season bulks, a review suggests a modest surplus of about 10 to 20% above maintenance for novice and intermediate lifters and a lower figure for advanced ones, with body-weight gain of about 0.25 to 0.5% per week for less advanced lifters; the authors note a study in which a larger surplus added more fat without a statistically significant extra muscle gain [2]. For cuts, a 2014 review proposes losing about 0.5 to 1% of body weight per week, with high protein intake to protect lean mass [9]. A randomized study of athletes found those losing about 0.7% of body weight per week gained lean mass, while a faster-loss group did not [9]. These are findings from the cited papers, not advice.

Practitioners say that a surplus is needed to drive growth beyond the early novice stage, that a deficit is needed to make the muscle visible, and that the swing between the two produces a better end result than staying at one body-fat level. Forum users debate when to switch phases and what body-fat range to target [4].

Critics inside and outside the lifting community raise other positions. Gaffney writes that there is little evidence bulking and cutting is superior for building muscle or losing fat over other methods, and the Cleveland Clinic's sports physician cites a study in which overeating produced the same muscle gain as a normal diet but more fat gain [3][5]. Reviews of bodybuilding nutrition note that the long-term evidence on off-season practice is limited [2].

Most research is on weight cycling in general populations, not lifters. Reviews describe a public perception that yo-yo dieting raises fat and lowers metabolic rate; a 2024 systematic review reported that most included studies found no such effect on BMI, fat mass, lean mass or resting metabolic rate [6]. The 2026 Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology review judged that adverse associations are likely circumstantial, citing ageing, unintentional weight loss, reverse causality and earlier onset of obesity [7]. Wikipedia lists meta-analyses linking weight fluctuation to higher cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, hypertension and new diabetes, and describes a pattern of disproportionate fat regain after weight loss [8].

For athletes, a Garthe and colleagues randomized trial reported that a slower rate of weight loss preserved or increased lean mass compared with a faster rate [9]. Gaffney notes that gradual weight loss better preserves resting metabolic rate, that extreme loss in people with obesity can lower it, and that bulking increases fat-cell number in some studies; he also cites a 2019 study in which 47% of 348 female bodybuilders had an eating disorder [3].

Larger surpluses add more fat; the Cleveland Clinic notes that excess calories stored as fat can contribute to high cholesterol and heart disease and that heavily processed diets can bring deficiencies and low energy [5]. Gaffney reports that high-calorie diets can raise cholesterol, blood sugar and liver fat over weeks [3].

In competitive bodybuilding, a review of natural competitors reports high rates of binge eating after contests (46% in one study), food preoccupation (81.5%) and muscle dysmorphia, and recommends access to mental-health professionals experienced with both bodybuilding and eating disorders [9]. A one-year case study of a natural bodybuilder recorded body mass rising about 10 kg during a six-month recovery after prep [9]. Roberts and colleagues recommend a controlled regain after prolonged dieting, warning that rapid regain tends to be mostly fat [10].

Muscle dysmorphia, the belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular, is classed within body dysmorphic disorder, with estimates of prevalence in studied male samples ranging widely and higher among bodybuilders and steroid users [11]. Wikipedia's bodybuilding article cites a 2025 study linking muscularity-focused social media content to muscle dysmorphia in boys and men [1].

A separate form of cycling occurs in weight-class sports. A 2024 systematic review of 26 survey studies with 3,994 participants from 14 combat sports found that weight loss for competition was highly prevalent, often begun as teenagers two to three times a year, usually involving less than 5% of body weight in 7 to 14 days, and that a minority use extreme practices [12]. A sports-medicine review of care for wrestlers also addresses rapid weight loss concerns [13]. Wikipedia notes that weight cycling is common in competitive combat sports, including among minors [8].

Looksmaxxing forums treat bulk and cut timing as a planning question tied to body-fat percentage, since leanness affects facial definition as well as physique [4]. Terms such as 'lean bulk' and 'clean bulk' are used alongside 'dirty bulk' in lifting communities, where the clean approach is described as limiting fat gain [1][5].

No clinical trial has tested lifters' bulk-and-cut cycles as a whole. Related human research covers weight cycling in general populations [6][7], slow versus fast weight loss in athletes [9], and off-season surplus size in trained lifters [2].

lore.intro: Lifters on forums discuss bulk and cut timing as a core planning question, with debate over target body-fat levels and clean versus dirty approaches [4][5].

Pumping Iron brings bodybuilding culture to a wide audience [1].
Garthe and colleagues publish a randomized trial comparing slow and fast weight loss in athletes [9].
Helms, Aragon and Fitschen publish evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation [9].
Iraki and colleagues publish a narrative review of off-season nutrition for bodybuilders [2].
Roberts and colleagues publish nutritional recommendations for physique athletes [10].
The Conversation publishes a physiologist's overview of bulking and cutting and metabolism [3].
A systematic review of 23 studies on the physiological effects of weight cycling appears in Current Obesity Reports [6].
A Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology review concludes evidence does not support a causal link between weight cycling and clinical harm [7].
